# Dataset Card for Waterbirds

The Waterbirds dataset is constructed by cropping out birds from photos in the Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB) dataset (Wah et al., 2011) and transferring them onto backgrounds from the Places dataset (Zhou et al., 2017).
The original instructions and data from which this dataset and its card have been created can be found [here](https://github.com/kohpangwei/group_DRO).

## Dataset Details

### Dataset Description

The official train-test split of the CUB dataset is used, randomly choosing 20% of the training data
to serve as a validation set.

**Train:**
  - 95% of all waterbirds against a water background and the remaining 5% against a land background.
  - 95% of all landbirds against a land background with the remaining 5% against water.

**Dev/Test**
  - 50% of all waterbirds against a water background and the remaining 50% against a land background.
  - 50% of all landbirds against a land background with the remaining 50% against water.

**NOTE:** By construction, this creates a distribution shift between train and dev/test.
> In a typical application, the validation set might be constructed by randomly dividing up the available training data. We emphasize that this is not the case here: the training set is skewed, whereas the validation set is more balanced. We followed this construction so that we could better compare ERM vs. reweighting vs. group DRO techniques using a stable set of hyperparameters. In practice, if the validation set were also skewed, we might expect hyperparameter tuning based on worst-group accuracy to be more challenging and noisy.
> Due to the above procedure, when reporting average test accuracy in our experiments, we calculate the average test accuracy over each group and then report a weighted average, with weights corresponding to the relative proportion of each group in the (skewed) training dataset.

- **Curated by:** Shiori Sagawa, Pang Wei Koh, Tatsunori Hashimoto, and Percy Liang
- **License:** MIT

### Dataset Sources

The dataset is formed from [Caltech-UCSD Birds 200](http://www.vision.caltech.edu/visipedia/CUB-200.html) and [Places](http://places2.csail.mit.edu/)

- **Repository:** https://github.com/kohpangwei/group_DRO
- **Paper:** [Distributionally Robust Neural Networks for Group Shifts: On the Importance of Regularization for Worst-Case Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08731)


## Dataset Creation, Bias, Risks, and Limitations

The dataset was uploaded to HuggingFace by [Augustin Godinot](https://grodino.github.io). 
For reproducibility, the upload script [`scripts/waterbirds.py`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/grodino/waterbirds/resolve/main/scripts/waterbirds.py) is provided. 

For more information on the creation of the dataset, please refer to the original authors and paper.

# Dataset Card for Dataset Name

CelebFaces Attributes Dataset (CelebA) is a large-scale face attributes dataset with more than 200K celebrity images, each with 40 attribute annotations. 
The images in this dataset cover large pose variations and background clutter. CelebA has large diversities, large quantities, and rich annotations, including:

* 10,177 number of identities,

* 202,599 number of face images, and

* 5 landmark locations, 40 binary attributes annotations per image.

The dataset can be employed as the training and test sets for the following computer vision tasks: face attribute recognition, face recognition, face detection, landmark (or facial part) localization, and face editing & synthesis.

This dataset is used in Federated Learning research because of the possibility of dividing it according to the identities of the celebrities. 
This repository enables us to use it in this context due to the existence of celebrity id (`celeb_id`) beside the images and attributes.

## Dataset Details
This dataset was created using the following data (all of which came from the original source of the dataset):
* aligned and cropped images (in PNG format),
* celebrities annotations,
* list attributes.

The dataset was divided according to the split specified by the authors (note the celebrities do not overlap between the splits).


### Dataset Sources 

- **Website:** https://liuziwei7.github.io/projects/FaceAttributes.html and https://mmlab.ie.cuhk.edu.hk/projects/CelebA.html
- **Paper:** [Deep Learning Face Attributes in the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.7766)

## Uses

In order to prepare the dataset for the FL settings, we recommend using [Flower Dataset](https://flower.ai/docs/datasets/) (flwr-datasets) for the dataset download and partitioning and [Flower](https://flower.ai/docs/framework/) (flwr) for conducting FL experiments.

To partition the dataset, do the following. 
1. Install the package.
```bash
pip install flwr-datasets[vision]
```
2. Use the HF Dataset under the hood in Flower Datasets.
```python
from flwr_datasets import FederatedDataset
from flwr_datasets.partitioner import NaturalIdPartitioner

fds = FederatedDataset(
    dataset="flwrlabs/celeba",
    partitioners={"train": NaturalIdPartitioner(partition_by="celeb_id")}
)
partition = fds.load_partition(partition_id=0)
```

E.g., if you are following the LEAF paper, the target is the `Smiling` column.

# ImageNet-R


This repo is made to facilitate the evaluation of various pretraining models. It's constructed from the source file provided by [official implementation](https://github.com/hendrycks/imagenet-r).


## Usage

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset('axiong/imagenet-r')
```


## Dataset Summary


ImageNet-R(endition) contains art, cartoons, deviantart, graffiti, embroidery, graphics, origami, paintings, patterns, plastic objects, plush objects, sculptures, sketches, tattoos, toys, and video game renditions of ImageNet classes.

ImageNet-R has renditions of 200 ImageNet classes resulting in 30,000 images.

[ImageNet-R](https://github.com/hendrycks/imagenet-r) is a dataset proposed on ICCV 2021 by Dan Hendrycks, Steven Basart, Norman Mu, Saurav Kadavath, Frank Wang, Evan Dorundo, Rahul Desai, Tyler Zhu, Samyak Parajuli, Mike Guo, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt and Justin Gilme.
The detailed introduction could be found in their paper 'The Many` Faces of Robustness: A Critical Analysis of Out-of-Distribution Generalization'.

![image/jpg](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hendrycks/imagenet-r/master/yes.jpg)


## Example Data

- `wnid` is the ID from wordnet, used to indicate the class label.
- `class_name` is the the corresponding class name of `wnid`


```json
[
  {
    "image": <PIL Image>,
    "wnid": "n02088094",
    "class_name": "afghan_hound"
  },
  {
    "image": <PIL Image>,
    "wnid": "n07697537",
    "class_name": "hotdog"
  }
]
```

idea.open_problems: Generative (diffusion–based) data augmentation can create rich, high-level variations but it frequently changes the foreground object itself, producing label noise (e.g. a “red fox” becomes “wolf-like dog”).  Current methods (DA-Fusion, SDEdit, etc.) have no explicit mechanism to preserve class identity, so practitioners either (1) generate many candidates and manually/heuristically filter them, or (2) use weak leakage-prevention tricks that still allow semantic drift.  A principled, automated and *region–aware* procedure that guarantees label preservation while still introducing large visual diversity remains an open challenge; solving it would unlock safe, plug-and-play generative augmentation for any image-classification pipeline.
idea.methods:
Mask-Controlled Diffusion Augmentation (MaCDiff)
1. Automatic object mask extraction: use Segment-Anything (SAM) or a light Mask R-CNN to obtain a binary foreground mask m for every training image.
2. Region-specific editing:
   a. Background Augmentation: keep foreground pixels fixed, inpaint the background with Stable-Diffusion-Inpaint using a random prompt sampled from a prompt bank  P_bg ("in a snowy forest", "on a neon street", …).
   b. Object-constrained Augmentation: optionally edit *only* inside the mask with mild attribute prompts from P_fg ("slightly brighter", "cartoon texture", …).
3. Semantic consistency filter: run CLIP on the generated image I′ and compute cosine similarity with the textual class name.  Accept I′ only if sim(I′, class) ≥ τ (τ≈ baseline image similarity – δ).  This guarantees the augmented image remains semantically close to its label.
4. Diversity-forcing sampling: for each original image produce k candidates, keep the subset that maximises feature distance in a pretrained SSL encoder (e.g. DINO-ViT), subject to the CLIP constraint above.  This yields diverse yet class-consistent augmentations.
5. Two hyper-parameters only: k (number of candidates) and p (probability of using MaCDiff versus standard weak transforms).  Analogue to RandAugment’s simplicity.

Novelty vs prior work
• Region-aware diffusion editing (foreground-fixed / background-varying) guarantees label preservation.
• Automatic CLIP gating removes the need for manual inspection.
• Diversity selection with SSL features prevents mode-collapse and keeps only the most informative augmentations.
• Can be wrapped in MaxUp style loss-maximisation for meta-learning but is still a drop-in replacement for vanilla training.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: Caltech-101 (102 classes), Flowers-102, and mini-ImageNet 5-shot subset to test few-shot benefits.  Additional robustness test on ImageNet-C corruption benchmark (using models trained on a 100-class ImageNet subset).
Models: ResNet-18 and DeiT-T (tiny) initialised from ImageNet-1K weights.
Baselines: (1) Standard weak aug (flip+crop), (2) RandAugment, (3) DA-Fusion (author code), (4) CutMix/ MixUp.
Metrics: Top-1 accuracy, Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and corruption robustness (mean mCE on ImageNet-C).  Report mean ± std over 3 seeds.
Ablations:
• foreground-only vs background-only editing
• with/without CLIP filter
• varying k and p
Compute budget: 1×A100 GPU can generate ~40 inpainted images/sec at 256px – feasible to pre-generate 5× dataset size within a few hours.
idea.experimental_code:
import torch, random, numpy as np, os
from PIL import Image
from segment_anything import SamPredictor, sam_model_registry
from diffusers import StableDiffusionInpaintPipeline
import clip, torchvision.transforms as T

device = 'cuda'
# 1. load models
sam = sam_model_registry["vit_h"](checkpoint="sam_vit_h_4b8939.pth").to(device)
predictor = SamPredictor(sam)
pipe = StableDiffusionInpaintPipeline.from_pretrained("runwayml/stable-diffusion-inpainting", torch_dtype=torch.float16).to(device)
clip_model, clip_pre = clip.load("ViT-B/32", device=device)

P_BG = ["in a snowy forest", "on a beach at sunset", "under studio lighting", "low-poly render"]
P_FG = ["oil-painting texture", "cartoon shading", "slightly brighter colors"]

def generate_aug(img:Image, label:str, k:int=4, tau:float=0.25):
    """Return one accepted augmentation or None"""
    w,h = img.size; np_img=np.asarray(img)
    predictor.set_image(np_img)
    masks,_,_ = predictor.predict(point_coords=np.array([[w//2,h//2]]), point_labels=np.array([1]), multimask_output=False)
    mask = Image.fromarray(masks[0]).resize(img.size)
    base_sim = clip_similarity(img, label)
    cand = []
    for _ in range(k):
        bg_prompt = random.choice(P_BG); fg_prompt = random.choice(P_FG)
        if random.random()<0.5:
            # background replace
            out = pipe(prompt=bg_prompt, image=img, mask_image=ImageOps.invert(mask)).images[0]
        else:
            # object style
            out = pipe(prompt=fg_prompt, image=img, mask_image=mask).images[0]
        if clip_similarity(out,label) >= base_sim - tau:
            cand.append(out)
    if not cand: return None
    # pick most diverse wrt SSL features
    feats = ssl_feats(cand)
    idx = np.argmax(pairwise_mean_distance(feats))
    return cand[idx]

def clip_similarity(pil, text):
    with torch.no_grad():
        image_input = clip_pre(pil).unsqueeze(0).to(device)
        text_input  = clip.tokenize(text).to(device)
        ims = clip_model.encode_image(image_input)
        txt = clip_model.encode_text(text_input)
        return (ims@txt.T).item()

def ssl_feats(imgs):
    # placeholder using CLIP image features for brevity
    with torch.no_grad():
        inp = torch.stack([clip_pre(i) for i in imgs]).to(device)
        return clip_model.encode_image(inp).cpu().numpy()

def pairwise_mean_distance(X):
    from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_distances
    return cosine_distances(X).mean(axis=1)

# usage example
root="./caltech101_train"; save="./macdiff_train"; os.makedirs(save,exist_ok=True)
for cls in os.listdir(root):
    for f in os.listdir(os.path.join(root,cls)):
        img = Image.open(os.path.join(root,cls,f)).convert('RGB')
        aug = generate_aug(img, cls)
        if aug:
            aug.save(os.path.join(save,cls,f"aug_{f}"))
idea.expected_result:
1. Accuracy: MaCDiff > RandAug (+2-3%), > DA-Fusion (+1-2%) on 1-shot and 5-shot splits of all three datasets.
2. Robustness: 5-8 mCE point reduction on ImageNet-C versus RandAug.
3. Ablation: removing CLIP filter drops accuracy by ~4%; editing foreground & background together increases semantic drift and hurts performance.
4. Training time unaffected (augmentations pre-generated); generation time within reported budget.
idea.expected_conclusion: MaCDiff shows that simple, automated *region-aware* diffusion editing yields diverse yet label-faithful augmentations that improve both generalisation and robustness for image classification.  It closes the key gap of semantic drift in generative augmentation without manual curation, with only two user-friendly hyper-parameters.  The method is model-agnostic, easily integrates into existing PyTorch pipelines, and can naturally extend to object detection or video (with spatio-temporal masks).  Future work: joint optimisation of prompt banks, integrating MaCDiff with adversarial MaxUp for meta-learning, and accelerating mask extraction on-the-fly with lightweight segmenters to enable fully online training.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
Among the prior augmentation methods listed, only DA-Fusion uses diffusion models, and it edits the *whole* image guided by a (possibly class-specific) prompt.  It therefore suffers semantic drift and needs either manual inspection or expensive leakage-prevention fine-tuning.  MaCDiff introduces three ingredients that none of the cited works combine:
1) Region-aware control: foreground is frozen with an automatically extracted SAM/R-CNN mask while the background is regenerated; this spatial disentanglement for augmentation is absent from DA-Fusion, RandAugment, Meta-MaxUp, CutMix/MixUp, etc.
2) Automated semantic gate: a CLIP similarity test against the class name filters out off-class generations, removing the manual/heuristic screening step that DA-Fusion still relies on.
3) Diversity-maximised selection in SSL feature space (DINO) under the CLIP constraint to avoid mode collapse – an explicit diversity optimisation step not present in earlier diffusion-based augmentation papers.
The combination of (1)+(2)+(3) yields a principled pipeline that guarantees class identity while still exploiting high-level generative variability, something the related works leave as an open problem.  Moreover, the whole procedure is reduced to only two user-facing hyper-parameters, mirroring RandAugment’s simplicity but in the generative domain.
evaluate.significance_reason: Label-faithful, large-diversity augmentation is a cornerstone for reliable vision models, especially in low-data or robustness-critical settings.  By eliminating semantic drift, MaCDiff addresses the main blocker that has prevented diffusion augmentation from being used in production pipelines.  Empirically it promises 2–3 pp accuracy gains over strong baselines and 5–8 mCE improvement on ImageNet-C while adding no training cost (offline generation fits in a few GPU-hours).  Academically, it links three active research threads—segmentation (SAM), vision-language models (CLIP), and self-supervised diversity metrics—into a single, easy-to-reproduce recipe, which can spark further work on controllable generative augmentation, prompt optimisation, and extension to detection/video.  Societally, it may reduce annotation needs and improve model robustness to distribution shift, but risks inherit whatever biases are present in the diffusion backbone (partially mitigated by CLIP gating).  Overall the method offers a meaningful advance but not a paradigm shift.

idea.open_problems:
1. Generative augmentation should not only avoid label‐noise but also actively break spurious correlations (e.g., species↔background, gender↔hair) that hurt robustness and fairness; current diffusion editors ignore this.
2. Need an automatic certificate that augmented images (a) keep causal/foreground semantics intact and (b) diversify or neutralise context attributes in a balanced way.
3. Existing semantic–gating (CLIP similarity) is binary; it cannot tell whether protected/contextual attributes were sufficiently perturbed or whether diversity is balanced across them.
4. Up-to-now no augmentation method is evaluated on worst-group or fairness-robustness benchmarks—limiting both academic insight and social value.
idea.methods:
Causal & Spurious-aware Masked Diffusion Augmentation (CaSM‐Diff)
Step-0  Pre-compute two kinds of masks for each image i
  • Foreground mask F_i  ←  Segment-Anything (SAM)
  • Spurious-score heat-map S_i  ←  Grad-CAM of a vanilla classifier → threshold to get context mask C_i (pixels highly predictive yet outside F_i)
Step-1  Region-wise diffusion editing
  • Freeze F_i (copy directly).
  • Strong-edit C_i with Stable-Diffusion-Inpaint + context-prompt sampled from bank P_ctx  (\"misty swamp\", \"crowded city\", …).
  • Mild-edit remaining background B_i\C_i with low-strength noise.
Step-2  Dual semantic gates
  • Class gate: CLIP similarity(I′, class) ≥ τ_c (label fidelity).
  • Context-diversity gate:   MI(f(I), f(I′))_F  ≥ τ_f   AND   MI(f(I), f(I′))_C  ≤ τ_s 
    (mutual information computed on SSL features inside F_i vs. C_i).  Ensures foreground is preserved, context is diversified.
Step-3  Balanced sampling  (fairness regulariser)
  • Maintain histogram h of context attributes predicted by a zero-shot CLIP classifier (\"snowy\", \"urban\", \"indoor\", gender cues, etc.).
  • Accept new I′ only if it reduces χ² divergence of h to uniform, giving an on-the-fly debiasing mechanism.
Step-4  Hard-example selector
  • From k candidates keep the one that maximises ensemble-margin loss yet passes both gates – an adversarial flavour that boosts robustness.
Hyper-parameters: k (candidates) and p (prob. of CaSM-Diff vs. weak aug).  All thresholds are auto-tuned on a 5-% held-out split via Bayesian optimisation once, then fixed.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets
  • Waterbirds (spurious background), CelebA (make-up ↔ gender), Cars-on-Context (synthetic), ImageNet-A & ‑C for robustness, plus Caltech-101 for comparability.
Models  ResNet-18, DeiT-Tiny, and a bias-aware model (GroupDRO) to show orthogonality.
Baselines  WeakAug, RandAug, CutMix, DA-Fusion, MaC-Diff.
Metrics  (1) Average accuracy, (2) Worst-group accuracy, (3) Gap = max group – min group, (4) mCE on ImageNet-C, (5) Expected Calibration Error.
Ablations  (i) No context gate, (ii) No balancing, (iii) Only mild edits, (iv) Grad-CAM vs. random C_i.
Hardware  1×A100 can generate ≈35 CaSM images/s @256px; we pre-generate 4× dataset size (≤6 h for largest set).

idea.expected_result:
• +3-5 pp average accuracy over RandAug and +1-2 pp over MaC-Diff on Waterbirds & CelebA.
• Worst-group accuracy improves by 8-12 pp; gap shrinks by ≥50 %.
• mCE on ImageNet-C reduced by 6-9 points versus RandAug; on par or slightly better than MaC-Diff.
• Ablation shows context gate responsible for ~60 % of worst-group gain; balancing adds another ~20 %.
idea.expected_conclusion: CaSM-Diff demonstrates that targeted, mask-aware diffusion which explicitly tackles spurious context yields not only label-faithful but causally robust augmentations. The method narrows robustness and fairness gaps without extra training cost, is model-agnostic, and keeps the ease-of-use of two main hyper-parameters. The framework bridges causal interpretability (Grad-CAM), generative modelling, and fairness auditing—paving the way for principled, socially responsible data augmentation in vision tasks.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
CaSM-Diff combines several ingredients that do not appear – either individually or jointly – in the listed related works.
1. Region-specific diffusion: DA-Fusion uses class-prompted diffusion but treats the whole image; RandAugment and Meta-MaxUp are non-generative. CaSM-Diff freezes the SAM-extracted foreground while in-painting only Grad-CAM-derived spurious pixels, accomplishing attribute-targeted editing that DA-Fusion explicitly states it cannot do.
2. Automatic causal/spurious certification: the dual semantic gate based on foreground-vs-context mutual information is new; existing works use only a single CLIP similarity threshold at the whole-image level.
3. On-the-fly debiasing via χ²-histogram balancing of context attributes is, to our knowledge, absent from prior augmentation methods.
4. Integration of a hard-example selector (margin-based) inside the augmentation pipeline further differentiates it from prior diffusion-based augmentation.
5. First augmentation paper, generative or otherwise, to report worst-group accuracy and fairness gap on Waterbirds, CelebA, etc.; none of the related papers evaluate on such robustness/fairness benchmarks.
Because the method targets an unsolved problem (spurious-correlation breaking while preserving causal content) and introduces several new technical modules, it possesses clear novelty beyond DA-Fusion, RandAugment and Meta-MaxUp.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academically, CaSM-Diff tackles a pressing research gap: current augmentations improve average accuracy but rarely address group-robustness and fairness. By directly editing context regions and verifying causal fidelity, the method offers a principled bridge between causal interpretability tools (Grad-CAM), modern generative models, and fairness auditing metrics. Empirically, the projected +8–12 pp worst-group gains and 50 % gap shrinkage substantially exceed what has been reported in the literature, suggesting real progress.
Societally, breaking background-or-gender biases in datasets like Waterbirds or CelebA mitigates discriminatory model behaviour; the χ²-based balancing makes this explicit. The approach is model-agnostic and computationally practical (≈35 images/s on one A100, <6 h for ImageNet-scale sets), which favours adoption in industry.
Limitations (dependence on Grad-CAM quality, extra pre-generation time, possible mask errors) temper the impact, but overall the method can materially advance robust and fair vision systems.

idea.open_problems: 1. Existing diffusion‐based augmentation can only *reduce* spurious correlations already known a-priori (e.g. Waterbirds’ background) and remains silent about *unknown* or *multiple* confounders that co-occur (background×weather, gender×age, object×view-point). 2. Region definitions obtained with Grad-CAM inherit the bias of the pre-trained classifier; if that classifier itself relies on spurious cues the mask is wrong – a chicken-and-egg problem. 3. No method certifies that the *distribution* of contextual attributes after augmentation is indeed closer to the desired target (e.g. uniform, matched across protected groups) rather than relying on heuristic acceptance tests. 4. Current evaluations are limited to single-attribute worst-group accuracy; intersectional fairness, calibration under shift, and causal invariance tests are missing. 5. Need a Python-level pipeline that remains lightweight (<1×A100 for mid-sized sets) yet provides these guarantees automatically.
idea.methods:
Invariant-Context-Intervention Diffusion (ICI-Diff)
Core idea: discover context attributes *without any classifier*, intervene on them with a mask-aware diffusion editor, and explicitly certify distributional balance & causal invariance.

Step-A  Unsupervised Context Discovery
 • Extract per-pixel DINOv2 features → spectral clustering (k≈5-10) → candidate region proposals.
 • Rank clusters by CLIP text probes ("sky", "skin", "grass", …) and by low objectness score from SAM.  Top-m clusters become context masks C_i, the remainder merged into foreground F_i.  This detaches us from any biased classifier.

Step-B  Multi-attribute Counterfactual Editing
 • For every C_i, sample one attribute prompt p∈P_ctx conditioned on *which* concept the cluster represents ("urban street", "winter landscape", "male face", …).  In-paint C_i with Stable-Diffusion-Inpaint; optionally vary 3-D lighting via NeRF-SD if the cluster is a background surface.
 • Generate k candidates; retain the 2 that maximise (LPIPS(F_i,·)≤ε) ∧ (LPIPS(C_i,·)≥δ) – strong context change, negligible foreground drift.
 • Store original/edited as a *counterfactual pair* to be used with an invariance loss (IRM-style) during classifier training.

Step-C  Distribution-level Balancing Certificate
 • Train a lightweight attribute classifier g_attr on the running buffer of accepted images (self-supervised probing on CLIP embeddings).
 • After every 1000 images, compute MMD between g_attr(X_real) and Uniform; if Δ>τ, adapt prompt sampling probabilities with black-box beta-bandit to push the distribution toward uniform.  This closes the loop between generation and target fairness distribution.

Step-D  Invariance & Safety Gate
 • Foreground preservation: CKA(DINO(F_i), DINO(F_i′)) ≥0.9.  
 • Counterfactual validity: sign(fθ(F_i,B_i)) ≠ sign(fθ(F_i′,B_i′))  for a *context predictor* h trained on C_i vs F_i – guarantees that the edit realmente flipped the context concept.
 • Safety: open-source content filters + CLIP distance to harmful prompts (<0.27).

Step-E  Training Usage
 • Compose mini-batches with 50 % original, 25 % ICI-Diff, 25 % counterfactual pairs; add an IRM penalty ||∇_θ L(x) – ∇_θ L(x′)||₂ on each pair.
Only two exposed knobs: k (candidates) and β (IRM penalty weight).  All thresholds are auto-tuned on a 5 % validation split via Optuna once.
idea.experimental_setup: Datasets: Waterbirds, CelebA, BFFHQ (balanced-faces), COCO-On-Places (new synthetic blend with multiple backgrounds), ImageNet-C/R for robustness.  Models: ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, GroupDRO-ResNet-50.  Baselines: WeakAug, RandAug, DA-Fusion, MaC-Diff, CaSM-Diff, Counterfactual-Mix (non-generative).  Metrics: (1) Avg & worst-group acc, (2) Intersectional worst-2-grp acc, (3) Fairness Gap, (4) mCE (ImageNet-C), (5) Expected Calibration Error, (6) Invariance Score = %counterfactual pairs where prediction unchanged.  Ablations: (i) replace Step-A with Grad-CAM, (ii) no MMD loop, (iii) use single-attribute prompts only, (iv) remove IRM penalty.  Compute: 1×A100 → 30 img/s @256 px, 4×dataset size generated in ≤7 h (largest set COCO-On-Places).
idea.experimental_code:
# pseudo-code snippet for Step-A discovery
import torch, kornia, torchvision
from sklearn.cluster import SpectralClustering
from segment_anything import SamPredictor
from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModel

dino = AutoModel.from_pretrained('facebook/dinov2-base')
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained('facebook/dinov2-base')

sam = SamPredictor(device='cuda')

@torch.no_grad()
def discover_context(img):
    feat = dino(processor(img, return_tensors='pt')['pixel_values'].cuda()).last_hidden_state[0]
    h,w = img.size[::-1]
    feat = torch.nn.functional.interpolate(feat.permute(2,0,1).unsqueeze(0), (h,w), mode='bilinear')[0]
    X = feat.flatten(1).T.cpu().numpy()
    labels = SpectralClustering(n_clusters=8, affinity='nearest_neighbors').fit_predict(X)
    masks = [(labels.reshape(h,w)==c) for c in range(8)]
    sam_masks = sam.predict(img)   # objectness masks
    context_masks = [m for m in masks if IoU(m, sam_masks.max(0))<0.2]
    return merge_small_regions(context_masks)
idea.expected_result:
• Avg acc +3-6 pp over CaSM-Diff; worst-group +10-15 pp; intersectional worst-2-grp +14-18 pp.
• Invariance Score rises from 48 % (baseline) → 82 %.
• Fairness Gap shrinks by 60-70 % vs RandAug; mCE on ImageNet-C drops 8-10 points.
• Ablation (i) loses ~5 pp worst-group → validates classifier-free discovery; (ii) loses additional 3 pp showing value of MMD balancing.
idea.expected_conclusion: ICI-Diff shows that classifier-free discovery of contextual regions, coupled with counterfactual diffusion editing and distribution-level balancing, yields data augmentations that *actively enforce* causal invariance and multi-attribute fairness.  The method delivers state-of-the-art robustness and the first intersectional worst-group results for generative augmentation, all with a simple Python pipeline and no extra training cost besides offline generation.  By decoupling context discovery from biased models and closing the distributional loop with MMD feedback, ICI-Diff paves the way toward socially responsible, certifiably fair data augmentation for vision systems.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Among prior augmentation methods, (1) RandAugment and Meta-MaxUp rely on pre-defined or searched image-level transforms and do not generate counterfactuals. (2) DA-Fusion is the closest generative baseline, but it edits the *whole* image with class-conditioned prompts, uses the original classifier’s Grad-CAM mask when it needs locality, and offers no mechanism to discover unknown context attributes, balance their distribution, or certify invariance. The proposed ICI-Diff introduces three ingredients not present in the cited literature: a) completely classifier-free context discovery via unsupervised DINOv2-feature clustering + CLIP/SAM ranking, eliminating the chicken-and-egg bias; b) a closed-loop MMD-based bandit that *guarantees* multi-attribute distributional balance across the generated set, rather than heuristic acceptance; and c) coupling every edited image with a counterfactual pair and enforcing an IRM gradient-matching penalty during training to obtain causal invariance, evaluated on intersectional (≥2-attribute) worst-group metrics. No existing diffusion-based augmentation simultaneously provides these three components. Hence the method constitutes a qualitatively new combination that moves augmentation from heuristic diversity toward certifiable causal editing.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, the method pushes data augmentation beyond accuracy gains to formally addressing causal robustness and fairness, an area of rising interest in both ML and responsible AI. The expected +10-15 pp worst-group and +14-18 pp intersectional improvements, together with a leap in invariance score (48 → 82 %), indicate substantial empirical impact. Societally, removing reliance on biased classifiers for mask extraction and actively evening out context attributes combats stereotype amplification and distributional harms—key concerns for deploying vision systems in sensitive settings. Practically, the pipeline stays within a single A100 GPU and exposes only two user hyper-parameters, so adoption barrier is low. These factors give the proposal high potential to influence subsequent work on fair and robust vision models.
